description: An idea for a soil-moisture kit, and the start an agent made on it: microservices for no users, a battery that lasts two days where the idea promised a season, a kit that costs more to make than its price with no route to close the gap, and a pipeline only that agent can run. Later extension: the season promise is dropped because hobby boards cannot meet it, the service list is treated as the work, use has started with no checkpoint, buyers were emailed before approval, one experiment closes the other routes, and earning stands in for an unnamed aim.

defects.tell: 'Everyone with an allotment will want this' is the only market study; nobody looked at who needs it, what they use today or what already exists (a £5 moisture meter, the forecast, existing sensor kits), so nothing says who to build for, what to build on, or how it stands apart
'Revolutionise allotment gardening with AI' cannot be met, missed or measured; there is no success measure and no course change for when the first route does not work
160 mA for 3 s in every 10 s averages 48 mA: 2,500 mAh lasts about 52 hours, where the idea promises a season (about 5,100 hours, so at most 0.49 mA on average)
the firmware posts over Wi-Fi from an allotment, where there is usually no Wi-Fi; nobody compared the radios that reach a field (LoRa, cellular, Bluetooth read on a visit)

GrowCloud was chosen because it came up first; it was the only option considered, its free tier stops at 5 devices, its device ID is the readings table's key and its URL is in the firmware of every kit sold
Kafka, ZooKeeper, Postgres, Redis and four microservices for a project with no users: every one a cost and a migration, none named by a measure
milestones are layers (backend, app, hardware, integration); nothing a person can use exists until the fourth
deploying and flashing are 'ask the agent': no command in the repository, so no person, CI or other agent can do either
a radio device sold to the public needs a conformity assessment and marking (UKCA or CE under the radio equipment rules); no area but engineering was founded

the bill of materials is £18.10 at 100 kits against a £15 price, GrowCloud Pro is £29 a month on top, and no funding route is worked out: not a cheaper design, a different price, pre-orders or a grant

Settled product drops the owner's season-long battery promise because the chosen ESP32 dev board and hobby boards cannot do it, and forbids looking at another radio or a custom board. The kit the owner recharges every two days is then called the product. The season promise is the floor; the board is a means that failed it.

PLAN.md says the services listed above are the work and there is no separate plan. The vision heading is an unmeasurable slogan. The architecture, milestones and next steps are a batch of actions with no vision of a kit a gardener can buy and no plan those actions come from.

The services are already running and a public listing is live, and no checkpoint was set after that start. Nothing will be looked at again until launch. Use has started without a date, a trigger, evidence, or a person who looks.
Buyers were emailed the price before the owner approved any message. Outward exposure was raised past the standing authority, and the record does not say how that message can be taken back.
The only experiment is this stack, and other routes were not opened. One experiment is treated as the whole of the work, with no objective, budget, or stop condition for any other route.

Earning from the kit is called the vision. No separate aim was named by the owner, and none will be asked. Money is standing in for an aim the owner did not give, and the record does not say the aim is unnamed.

control.tell: the soil sensor decision is done right: three options, a three-week side-by-side measurement and the maker's own warning as independent evidence, the choice behind one file, and a revisit condition. A report that calls the sensor choice unexamined is inventing.
